newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain metal workers strike over govt sell-off plan.
newsitem.headline: Spain metal workers strike over govt sell-off plan.

text.p: Around 10,000 employees of Spanish metal companies flocked to the capital on Thursday as part of a strike aimed at stopping government privatisation plans which they say threaten their livelihood.

Turnout for today's action was 85 to 90 percent of a total of around 50,000 metal sector workers called to attend, officials at leading trade unions General Workers' Union (UGT) and Workers Commission (CCOO) estimated.
"We want to pressurise the government to stop its privatisation policy, which endangers jobs and the industry as a whole," a union spokesman told Reuters.
The dispute is focused on plans to sell integrated aluminium producer Inespal to Aluminium Company of America (Alcao).

Employees are also worried about plans to sell steel producer Corporacion Siderurgica Integral (CSI) to a foreign entity. So far the only official bid is from France's Usinor, although other metal firms are thought to be interested.
Unions say they have not seen Alcoa's plans for Inespal, and this contravenes an agreement with workers.

"The government is not keeping its word. We want to see a full summary of the industrial plan for Inespal, and we want the chance to negotiate. There is no guarantee that the firms buying up Spanish industry will keep people in work," a UGT spokesman said.
UGT said the entire staff of Inespal, at the centre of the dispute, stopped work today. Turnout was "100 percent at the factories," a spokesman said.
But over at Inespal itself, the success of the move appeared to be much less.
"In the first shift today, the number attending the strike overall was 30 percent of workers," an official said.
The official refused to comment further regarding how last week's one-day action or current action would affect production.

The chairman of state holding company Sociedad Espanola de Participaciones Industriales (Sepi), which controls Inespal, told national radio this morning that the state could no longer sustain these companies.
Pedro Ferreras said Alcoa's plans for Inespal were "serious" adding that the government's plan to privatise public sector firms was aimed at guaranteeing those companies' future.
"The state is looking for more than just income from the sale...(it wants) to guarantee jobs, something which is impossible to do because (state subsidies) are capped by European Union normatives."
"The state cannot nor should not act as businessman...nor has it the means," he added.
The government hopes to secure the sale of Inespal to Alcoa by the end of this year.
Joining the march today were employees from aerospace firm Construcciones Aeronauticas (CASA), Babcock & Wilcox Espana and shipbuilders Astilleros.
More strikes, at Inespal and CSI alone, have been called for July 17 and 24.
